protocol.instrument_name: NSW Pharmacist Practice Standards for Acute Nausea and Vomiting
protocol.instrument_version: Authority dated 05 August 2026; document approved 05 AUGUST 2026 (no version number printed)
protocol.legal_basis: 'Approved medicines listed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 05 August 2026) are: a. Ondansetron b. Metoclopramide' (p2). 'Pharmacists must hold general registration under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (NSW) and have successfully completed the training requirements detailed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 05 August 2026).' (p2) Approved by Dr Kerry Chant AO PSM, Chief Health Officer and Deputy Secretary, Population and Public Health, 05 AUGUST 2026 (p16).
protocol.supervision_model: approved pharmacist - 'Patients are required to have a consultation with an approved pharmacist before a medication can be supplied under the Authority.' (p4) 'Patients must be physically present in the pharmacy to be eligible for management.' (p4) The flowchart refers to a 'participating approved pharmacist' (p3). The document does not use 'collaborative' or 'autonomous' terminology and states no supervision or endorsement requirement beyond general registration and completion of Authority training.
protocol.scope_summary: NSW Health practice standard for pharmacists managing acute nausea and vomiting in patients aged 18 years and over under the Community Pharmacy Acute Nausea and Vomiting Service: two approved oral medicines (ondansetron, metoclopramide) with a maximum of 24-hours' supply of oral preparations of a single approved medicine, a patient assessment flowchart, a 29-row urgent referral criteria table (Section G), patient history/examination/BSL assessment (Section I), management and treatment plan including off-label ondansetron consent and metoclopramide/prochlorperazine/promethazine restrictions (Section J), counselling, documentation, TGA adverse event reporting and My Health Record upload.

steps.description: 'Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of acute nausea and vomiting'. 'The following flowchart should be used in consultations to assess the eligibility, identity and govern supply of suitable treatments, and guide associated referral requirements.'
Flowchart gate: 'Is the patient >=18 years old?' No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standard. Refer to GP.'

gates.criterion: Patient is 18 years of age or older

steps.description: Flowchart gate: 'Does the patient have any red flags, or exclusions?' Yes: proceed to PW-1-S4 ('Check Section G ... to determine if patient may be treated and/or must be referred for GP or ED management.'). No: continue to consent (PW-1-S5).

gates.criterion: Patient has no red flags or exclusions (Section G)

steps.description: 'Check Section G (Patient eligibility and referral criteria) to determine if patient may be treated and/or must be referred for GP or ED management.' Section G: 'Patients who meet any of the urgent referral criteria below are not eligible for this service and require immediate referral to their regular medical practitioner, health service, or Emergency Department (ED) as indicated in the table.'

gates.criterion: Patient meets none of the urgent referral criteria in Section G

steps.description: 'Obtain patient informed consent: Participation / Financial / Pharmacist communication with other health practitioners'. No consent branch: 'Pharmacist must not proceed to provide management under the Authority and Practice Standard. Refer to GP in circumstances of declined consent.'

gates.criterion: Informed consent obtained (participation, financial, and pharmacist communication with other health practitioners)

steps.description: 'Conduct patient history and clinical review including review of contraindications, precautions, drug interactions, pregnancy and lactation status'
'Establish management plan'
'Communicate agreed management plan with patient and patient's medical practitioner. Document all aspects of management plan.'

diagnosis_pathways.name: Patient history, examination and investigation (Section I)

steps.description: 'A patient history and examination that is tailored to the patient's presentation is required to inform the management approach, including appropriate referral. The prompts provided below are not exhaustive, pharmacists should maintain an open mind and be aware of cognitive bias.'
'Sufficient information must be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of management. The My Health Record should be reviewed where appropriate and available.'

'History of the presenting concern, including onset, and duration of symptoms, the timing of nausea and vomiting in relation to meals, and the frequency, amount, and content (liquid, solid, bile, blood (including “coffee ground” appearance)) of vomitus to identify a cause.'

'Associated symptoms, including pain (in particular abdominal pain, chest pain, or headache), neurological symptoms (such as blurred vision, vertigo, confusion, neck stiffness, photophobia, and presence of non-blanching rash), and the frequency and characteristics of stool (including presence and character of diarrhoea or constipation).' 'If abdominal pain is present, exploration of the character, duration, frequency, time of occurrence, location and distribution, and any exacerbating and relieving factors that may indicate an intraabdominal cause.'

'Associated history, including any symptoms in household or other close contacts, recent travel, potential exposure to food poisoning sources, recent weight loss, and recent head trauma/injury.' (bullet continues from page 7 onto page 8)
'Assessment of clinical status including fluid input and output, level of consciousness, and presence of fever and other signs of infection.'

'Pregnancy assessment, noting that patients may not be aware that they are pregnant, particularly as nausea / vomiting commonly occurs in early gestation. If they confirm they are pregnant, ask about gestation and any relevant pregnancy history. Incorporate the PUQE-24 tool as part of the assessment of pregnant women.'

'Past medical history including gastrointestinal, neurological, and metabolic/endocrine conditions (including diabetes mellitus).' 'Surgical history, including any recent abdominal surgical procedures.' 'Medication and allergy history, including recent commencement or cessation of medications, and any medications or therapies taken to address current symptoms.' 'Drug and alcohol history.' 'Mental health history, noting that nausea and vomiting may be functional, or associated with eating disorders such as bulimia.'

'A clinical examination should be guided by the patient's history, and conducted to identify potential causes, exclude life-threatening conditions, and assess potential sequelae, including the patient's level of dehydration. It is important to note that symptoms of severe dehydration and shock are also present in sepsis.' 'A physical examination should be conducted as appropriate (e.g. abdominal examination). ... there should be a low threshold for referral for medical care where signs and symptoms are unclear.'

'The patient's level of dehydration should be assessed, in line with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Assessing adults for dehydration, including vital signs as appropriate.' Notes: 'while moderate to severe dehydration is often associated with low blood pressure (hypotension), high blood pressure (hypertension) in a patient who is pregnant may be a sign of pre-eclampsia.' 'In older patients, traditional symptoms and signs of dehydration may be absent ... Symptoms and signs can include increased confusion, functional decline, chest pain, and falls.'

'A blood sugar level (BSL) is recommended for all patients and must be performed on any patient who has a history of diabetes. A high BSL may be a sign of diabetic ketoacidosis, which requires referral to emergency health services for review and management. Patients on SGLT inhibitors may present with euglycemic ketoacidosis. As such, there should be a lower threshold for referral to urgent medical care in this group.'

gates.criterion: BSL performed on any patient who has a history of diabetes

steps.description: 'Any patient presenting with signs and symptoms of a life-threatening condition, including severe dehydration, diabetic ketoacidosis, or an acute abdomen, must be referred to an emergency department for urgent review and management.' 'Where there is doubt of the cause of acute nausea and vomiting, the severity of dehydration, or the presence of life-threatening conditions, the patient must be referred for medical review.'

gates.criterion: No signs or symptoms of a life-threatening condition (including severe dehydration, diabetic ketoacidosis, or an acute abdomen)

diagnosis_pathways.name: Management, treatment plan and documentation (Sections J and K)

steps.description: 'It is important to identify, treat, or remove the cause of acute nausea and vomiting, as well as ensure adequate hydration before starting treatment of symptoms.'

'Refer patients for medical review if they have any red flags or other indications for referral (see tables). Where the cause of acute nausea and vomiting is unclear, patients should also be referred for medical review.'

gates.criterion: Patient has no red flags or other indications for referral and the cause of acute nausea and vomiting is identified

steps.description: 'For patients who have a history and examination consistent with viral gastroenteritis, it is important to provide advice to minimise the risk of transmission, including hand hygiene, food safety practices, and avoidance of high-risk settings such as aged care facilities until at least 24-48 hours after their diarrhoea or vomiting have resolved.'

'Managing hydration status is one of the most important aspects of acute nausea and vomiting. Rehydration should be aligned with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Rehydration for acute gastroenteritis in adults. Adults with features of mild to moderate dehydration can usually be adequately managed with oral rehydration (water and/or rehydration drinks). Drinks that are high in sugar may worsen diarrhoea if this is present.'
'Patients should be encouraged to eat as normally as possible, with small, light meals, as guided by their appetite. Fatty, spicy or heavy foods may worsen symptoms.'

'Nausea and vomiting can often be effectively managed with non-pharmacological therapy, including dietary changes, appropriate hydration, and rest.' 'If using pharmacotherapy, the choice of antiemetic should be determined by the clinical situation, noting that there are a number of neural pathways implicated in nausea and vomiting.'

'Pharmacotherapy for the control of symptoms in acute nausea and vomiting under this Practice Standard must be in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Nausea and Vomiting, and the following: A maximum of 24-hours' supply of oral preparations of a single approved medicine may be given to patients. This does not preclude the use of prochlorperazine or promethazine hydrochloride under pre-existing Schedule 3 indications, or any other Schedule 3 anti-emetics, that fall outside of this Practice Standard.'

gates.criterion: Supply does not exceed a maximum of 24-hours' supply of oral preparations of a single approved medicine (unless a higher quantity specified in the Authority)

steps.description: 'Ondansetron is currently approved by the TGA for the prevention of nausea and vomiting induced by cytotoxic therapy and radiotherapy, and for the prevention of post-operative nausea and vomiting. Use for nausea and vomiting outside of these indications is considered off-label use. The pharmacist must provide sufficient information to enable informed consent, including explaining the off-label nature of the use and the rationale for treatment. Informed consent must be obtained prior to supply and documented in the clinical record.'

gates.criterion: Off-label nature of ondansetron use and rationale explained, informed consent obtained prior to supply, and documented in the clinical record

steps.description: 'Metoclopramide as a dopamine antagonist, metoclopramide is associated with extrapyramidal adverse effects (EPSEs), usually acute dystonic reactions. EPSEs are more common in the elderly, people under 20 years of age, and people with renal failure. Metoclopramide must not be given to patients under 20 years of age, patients with Parkinson's Disease, or patients with suspected gastrointestinal obstruction.'

gates.criterion: Patient is 20 years of age or older, does not have Parkinson's Disease, and does not have suspected gastrointestinal obstruction before metoclopramide is given

steps.description: 'Prochlorperazine is particularly useful for acute nausea and vomiting associated with migraine, motion sickness, or acute gastroenteritis. It is available as a Schedule 3 medicine for the treatment of acute nausea and vomiting associated with migraine. As a dopamine antagonist, it can also cause EPSEs, including tardive dyskinesia and akathisia. It must not be given to patients who have Parkinson's disease.'

gates.criterion: Patient does not have Parkinson's disease before prochlorperazine is given

steps.description: 'Promethazine Hydrochloride is an antihistamine with antiemetic effects, and available as a Schedule 3 medicine. It can cause sedation, lower the seizure threshold and have anticholinergic effects. It can also cause EPSEs, including tardive dyskinesia; and should not be given to patients who have Parkinson's disease.'

gates.criterion: Patient does not have Parkinson's disease before promethazine hydrochloride is given

steps.description: 'Concurrent use of metoclopramide and prochlorperazine increases the risk of EPSE, including acute dystonic reactions, and is not recommended. Pharmacists must assess for current or recent use of dopamine antagonist antiemetics before supplying treatment under this Practice Standard.'

gates.criterion: No current or recent use of dopamine antagonist antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) that would increase the risk of EPSE when supplying treatment

steps.description: 'Additional consideration should be taken when managing nausea and vomiting in patients who are pregnant, in line with the NSW Health Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum. This includes appropriate recognition and referral of patients with severe, persistent, or late onset nausea and vomiting, as well as consideration of appropriate non-pharmacological and pharmacological therapies depending by symptom pattern and gestational age.'

'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, and other relevant references should be provided to the patient regarding: Individual product and medicine use, including contraindications and precautions; How to manage adverse effects; Supportive care, including the importance of rehydration; The impact of vomiting on the absorption and effectiveness of other regular medications; When to seek further care and/or treatment from a medical practitioner, including recognising signs and symptoms of “red flags” and dehydration. All patients should be advised to seek medical care if their symptoms worsen or do not improve with 24-48 hours.'
'The agreed management plan must be documented in the patient electronic clinical record and shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary team, in accordance with the Authority.'

gates.criterion: Agreed management plan documented in the patient electronic clinical record

steps.description: 'Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.'

gates.criterion: Details of the supply uploaded to the patient's My Health Record unless the patient requests otherwise

steps.description: 'Repeat clinical review with the pharmacist is generally not required. Patients should be advised to seek medical care if their symptoms worsen, or do not improve or resolve within 24-48 hours.'

'The pharmacist must make an electronic clinical record, and a record in a pharmacy dispensing system regarding the supply of any medications under these services, in accordance with the Authority.' 'Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.'

gates.criterion: Electronic clinical record and pharmacy dispensing system record made for the supply of any medications under these services

provenance.section_heading: G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA

routine: Patients who have requested the service but are not eligible for management should be referred to their regular medical practitioner or health service.
Patients who require non-urgent referral to GP or maternity provider are to be referred (in accordance with the usual referral processes).
Pharmacists must apply clinical judgement and refer any patient considered appropriate for medical care for any reason.
Refer to GP. (declined consent - flowchart, p3)

When nausea and vomiting in pregnancy is within scope for treatment ... treatment should be accompanied by a referral to the patient's GP and/or existing maternity care provider for ongoing management.
urgent: Urgent: GP or maternity care provider
emergency: A patient presenting with a potentially life-threatening cause for their acute nausea and vomiting must be immediately referred to emergency health services for urgent review and management.

Any patient presenting with signs and symptoms of a life-threatening condition, including severe dehydration, diabetic ketoacidosis, or an acute abdomen, must be referred to an emergency department for urgent review and management.

open_questions.observed: The text layer of the Section D flowchart interleaves box text and branch labels (e.g. 'Not eligible for management ... Is the patient ≥18 years old? No ... Standard. Refer to GP.'), so box/branch ordering was reconstructed from the fragments.
open_questions.why_unclear: Layout information is lost in text extraction; ordering of boxes and Yes/No branch labels is inferred rather than read directly.

open_questions.observed: Both tables on pages 5-6 have columns 'Referral criteria | Treat | Referral' (and 'Details of presenting complaint' with Treat values Yes/No/Yes*). Rows with Treat: No were transcribed as exclusions; rows with Treat: Yes (with a referral) as exclusion_exceptions.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not print a legend defining the 'Treat' column; the reading (Treat=No means the pharmacist must not supply) is inferred from context.

open_questions.observed: Section G spans pages 4-6 and the red flag table continues from page 5 to page 6; the referral block provenance uses page 4 (first page of Section G).
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires a single provenance page for the referral block; range noted here per spec.

open_questions.topic: No dose information printed for approved medicines
open_questions.observed: Neither ondansetron nor metoclopramide has a strength, dose, form, frequency or duration printed anywhere in the document; pharmacotherapy 'must be in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Nausea and Vomiting' and the NSW Health Authority (dated 05 August 2026).
open_questions.why_unclear: Dosing is held outside this document; no numeric dosing can be transcribed without inventing content.

open_questions.observed: Red flag row prints 'Altered level of conscious' (apparently truncated; likely 'consciousness').
open_questions.why_unclear: Printed text appears incomplete; transcribed verbatim without correction.

open_questions.observed: The urgent referral table lists 'Patients taking SGLT inhibitors' as 'Urgent: GP' (Treat: No), while Section I states there should be 'a lower threshold for referral to urgent medical care in this group'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Two different urgency readings recorded without reconciliation, per spec rule 2.

open_questions.observed: No version number is printed; the document cites 'NSW Health Authority (dated 05 August 2026)' and is signed 'Approved ... 05 AUGUST 2026' (p16).
open_questions.why_unclear: Version identifier absent; effective_date set from the printed approval date.

open_questions.observed: Heading prints as 'K. CLINICAL DOCUMENATION AND COMMUNICATION' (sic); used verbatim as section_heading.
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed as printed rather than corrected.

open_questions.topic: Table title placement and rotated text
open_questions.observed: Table titles 'Red flag warning signs' (p5) and 'Details of presenting complaint' (p6) appear reversed/rotated in the text layer; the red flag table on page 6 continues without the page-5 title.
open_questions.why_unclear: Rotated title text confirmed by reversing the extracted strings; section_heading for page-6 rows uses the printed column header 'Referral criteria'.

open_questions.observed: 'The patient is pregnant and is 16 weeks' gestation or more' has its referral cell wrapping onto the next line as 'or maternity care provider'; read as 'Urgent: GP or maternity care provider'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Row cell boundaries are ambiguous in the text layer; confidence marked medium.

open_questions.observed: Row 'The patient is <20 years of age and cannot receive any other anti-emetic other than metoclopramide | Treat: No | GP' read as a supply exclusion (EXC-31), while metoclopramide itself is prohibited under 20 years (p10).
open_questions.why_unclear: The phrase 'cannot receive any other anti-emetic other than metoclopramide' implies an alternative-anti-emetic check whose criteria are not printed.
